title: Voting Systems
objective: After this level you can compare winner-take-all and proportional voting.
summary: FPTP elects each district's top vote-getter; PR matches seats to votes; ranked systems transfer preferences. New Zealand moved to MMP. Arrow showed every system trades something.

cards.headline: In 1978, one New Zealand party won the most votes. The other one won power.
cards.body: It happened again in 1981. Both times Labour won more votes nationwide, but National won more seats and kept governing, and criticism of the voting system grew. How can that happen? It depends on how votes turn into seats.

cards.headline: First past the post
cards.body: In first-past-the-post, used in the UK, Canada, India and the United States, each district elects one member: whoever gets the most votes, majority or not. Win lots of districts narrowly and you can take more seats with fewer votes. In the 1950s the political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that this system tends to squeeze politics into two big parties.

cards.headline: Proportional representation
cards.body: Proportional representation aims straight at New Zealand's problem: a party's share of the votes becomes a matching share of seats. Districts elect several members; in Israel and the Netherlands the whole country is one district. New Zealand switched. A Royal Commission recommended Germany's mixed system (MMP) in 1986, and from 1996 voters got two votes: one for a local MP, one for a party.

cards.headline: Ranked choice
cards.body: Ranked systems ask for more than one choice. Australia's House of Representatives uses the Alternative Vote: rank the candidates, and if nobody has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes pass to next preferences until someone does. Ireland's Single Transferable Vote uses rankings in districts that elect several members, keeping results fairly proportional.

items.label: First past the post
points: Simple, with a clear local member

items.label: Proportional
points: Few wasted votes; smaller parties get in

items.label: Arrow's warning
points: 1951: no way of combining rankings meets every fairness condition at once
It won him a Nobel Prize in 1972

mascot.line: The IDEA handbook's trade-offs plus Arrow's proof: choosing a voting system means choosing which flaw you can live with.

cards.headline: Voting systems: compared
learned: FPTP: most votes in each district wins the seat
Duverger: FPTP tends toward two big parties
PR: seats match vote shares; coalitions are common
Ranked systems transfer votes by preference

questions.prompt: Under first-past-the-post, who wins a district's seat?

options.label: Only a candidate with over half the votes
options.rationale: FPTP needs the most votes, not a majority.

options.label: The candidate with the most votes, even without a majority
Parties share the seat by vote share
options.rationale: One member per district; no sharing.

options.label: Whoever leads after preferences are transferred

questions.explanation: In first-past-the-post, each district elects the candidate with more votes than any other, majority or not.

questions.prompt: According to the trade-offs in this level, what do critics most often say proportional systems lead to?

options.label: Smaller parties being shut out
options.rationale: That's the usual criticism of FPTP.

options.label: Large numbers of wasted votes
options.rationale: PR is praised for wasting very few votes.

options.label: A strict two-party system
options.rationale: Duverger linked two parties to FPTP.

questions.explanation: PR wastes few votes and lets smaller parties in, but critics say it tends to bring coalitions and fragmented parties.

questions.prompt: New Zealand's 1978 and 1981 results (more votes, fewer seats) fed criticism of its system. What did the country eventually adopt?

options.label: A second round of voting in each district
options.rationale: New Zealand chose a proportional system instead.

options.label: A ban on third parties
options.rationale: New Zealand made its system more proportional, not less.

options.label: Presidential elections
options.rationale: The change was to how Parliament is elected.

options.label: Germany's mixed member proportional system, MMP

questions.explanation: A Royal Commission recommended Germany's MMP in 1986, and New Zealand first voted under it in 1996.
